title: Master Class | French Defense | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The pawn to e4, e6 — a French, against David Vest.
d4 — you already know what we play against the French.
d5, and we play e5 — the Advance.
He goes b6 — an alternative to the main move c5; the idea is to get the bishop out to a6.
To slow down, in fact prevent entirely, the bishop to a6, we play c3 —
— a move we normally play in the Advance.
How does c3 prevent the bishop to a6? Because if the bishop to a6, we take it and play the queen to a4 with check, picking off the knight.
c6. Now there's nothing particularly special we have to do against the bishop threat —
— we just want to develop our pieces nicely, starting with the bishop to d3.
a5. Now let's think about where to put this knight — f3 or e2? If you've watched my French games, you know I have an affinity for e2 —
— the knight to e2, because I like keeping the f-pawn free to charge Black's pawn chain, with f4 and f5 later, since the e6-pawn could get under tremendous pressure.
But first we complete our development — we don't want to rush with f4. The bishop to a6.

Let's castle and do all the nice things, then when we're ready go f4 and try for f5. The queen takes d3, a4 — he's expanding on the queenside without developing, so we press the gas. He could meet f4 with g6, creating kingside weaknesses we could exploit. The knight to h6 stops f5; our idea is the f5 pawn break. In a closed centre nothing happens quickly against good players — you have to be methodical. We could go the knight to g3, but he plays g6; the knight to d2 is patient, but I like a more direct idea to contest f5 — h3, reserving the option of g4.

Now that we've played g4, we can play the knight to g3 with a clean conscience, and everything is finally ready for a5 and the f5 break — though after c5, f5 comes with a lot of risk, so I make a ridiculous-looking move: the knight back to b1. The main idea is to unblock the bishop, because when Black attacks the d4-pawn I don't want it to collapse — that pawn holds our whole position together. So the bishop can go to e3 to protect it, and the knight redirects from b1 to c3, a more active square than d2, with the rook coming to c1 — retooling the queenside to defend d4 and coordinate. He goes the queen to b5, and this is a great chance to strike: don't care about the b2-pawn, just play the knight to c3, and if the queen takes b2, protect the knight with a rook and start threatening discoveries and sacrifices, since his kingside is undeveloped. The rook to c1 creates an x-ray against the knight — tactical potential everywhere, and f5 is still available. He plays g6, and now f5 — the point isn't to open a file but to create a pathway: with g6 gone, h5 is no longer controlled, so the knight goes to h5 and heads for the juicy f6 outpost; g5 forcing the knight back to g8 was also possible, and the bishop to g5 pins the knight if the king goes to d8. He plays the knight to g8 to prevent the knight to f6 — but does it? The Sam Shankland question, what if I do it anyway: the knight to f6 with check, the knight takes f6, the pawn recaptures, and that f6-pawn is almost as strong as a knight, forcing the e7-knight out and leaving the king on e8 wide open, with a sacrifice on d5 to open a file for the rook. He plays the knight to c8, and we have a discovery against the knight — the knight takes d5 is best with tempo, so first the rook to f2, getting the queen back to b4; if the queen to a3, the knight to b5 forks and wins. The queen to b4, and we break through — patience pays off. The queen to d6; we take the knight, and now, with our rook and knight both hanging, the rook to c2, the queen takes d5, the knight to b6, the queen takes b6, and the knight to e7 fulfills every task — he can't take it without losing the rook, the problem with being undeveloped. We're up a rook, the bishop takes f6 or h7, and it's over; the king to e7, and finally, after all this time, we take on f5 to open the file, e5, take, and the rest wins itself.
b6 is an old system that's existed for a long time. Let's analyze the game.
Why did I play c3? Because he's trying to play the bishop to a6 and trade off the French bishop, which Black always wants to get rid of —
— could we go the queen to a4 with check immediately? Move order is extremely important. What would happen if we did, and is it sufficient —

— unfortunately Black has the queen to d7 here, hitting our queen; we don't have time to take the bishop, we have to respond to the tension, and after the queen trade and the king recaptures, Black is out of the woods.
So in such situations you often have to do the trade first —
— take on a6, and then you can actually win the knight.
Black plays c6 to cover the diagonal — that's the idea.
The bishop to d3.
— the point of a5 is to expand on the queenside —
— and also so that after the bishop to a6, the knight there won't be easily attacked.
The knight to d2 — I don't like the way Black is playing.
This is how you play the system, but I think it's extremely dubious.

So we castle, takes, takes, a4 — Black continues not to develop, so we bang the gas: f4, the knight to h6, and now h3. A lot of you suggest the tempting knight to g3 to prepare f5, but after g6 the f5 break is very hard — we'd love a pawn on g4 to make f5 realistic; h3 is a much more direct way to prepare the kingside attack. The queen to c8, we go g4, Black plays g6, and now the very patient knight to d2 — just develop, no need to rush f5, depending on how much material you stand to win.
